sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation and Initial Stabilization of Severe Anaphylaxis
sections.description: The case begins with a woman in her 60s presenting to the emergency department (ED) with a life-threatening systemic reaction, marking her first documented episode of anaphylaxis. Her background includes significant comorbidities, specifically type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, psoriasis, and depression, alongside a notable history of drug allergies. While she experienced a mild localized reaction to amoxicillin in adolescence and a strong local reaction to a wasp sting without systemic involvement, her current presentation represents a dramatic escalation in severity. The precipitating event occurred five days prior to admission when she was treated for erysipelas with clindamycin, which induced a delayed cutaneous rash. sections.section_title: Defining Biphasic and Multiphasic Anaphylaxis: Pathophysiology and Diagnostic Challenges
sections.description: Understanding the evolution of anaphylaxis requires moving beyond the immediate recognition of the initial hypersensitivity event to appreciating its dynamic temporal profile. Clinicians must distinguish between a monophasic course, characterized by a single episode of symptoms resolving completely, and complex courses involving recurrence. **Biphasic anaphylaxis** is formally defined as the spontaneous return of anaphylactic symptoms hours after the initial reaction has resolved, occurring in the absence of further allergen exposure. When this pattern extends to multiple distinct episodes of relapse, as seen in our case patient who experienced four separate shock events over 12 hours, it is classified as **multiphasic anaphylaxis**. sections.section_title: Diagnostic Reasoning in Complex Relapsing Courses and Underlying Etiologies
sections.description: The clinical trajectory of this patient illustrates a profound diagnostic challenge: distinguishing between a standard biphasic anaphylactic reaction and a more complex, multiphasic course driven by an underlying mast cell disorder. Upon the patient's first relapse of anaphylactic shock while monitored on the acute internal ward, the decision to transfer to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) was driven by the failure of intermittent rescue therapy to provide sustained stability. Although the patient responded adequately to intramuscular epinephrine, the recurrence of life-threatening hemodynamic collapse indicated that the inflammatory cascade was self-perpetuating rather than resolving spontaneously.
